grading_rubric.correct: Answer matches the reference on every required fact; no false additions; appropriate hedging when the context itself reports a gap.
grading_rubric.partially_correct: Some required facts present and accurate, but at least one required fact missing OR at least one wrong fact added.
grading_rubric.incorrect: Most required facts missing or wrong; or confidently states something the source contradicts.

questions.question: Describe the schema and population logic of the `other_procedures` column. List the inner struct fields in order, where each comes from, and explain how `procedure_<i>_type` is computed.
questions.reference_answer: `other_procedures` is an `array<struct>` built from up to MAX_PROC=4 ranked procedure records. For each rank i (1..4) a struct is wrapped in `when(col(f'procedure_{i}_code').isNotNull(), struct(...))`, collected via `array(*proc_structs)` into `other_procedures_raw`, then `other_procedures = filter(other_procedures_raw, x -> x is not null)` drops the absent ranks. The inner struct has 8 fields in this order: (1) `reference_id` = `lit(None).cast('string')` (always NULL placeholder); (2) `codeset` = `procedure_{i}_code`; (3) `codeset_display` = `procedure_{i}_description`; (4) `modifier_code` = `procedure_{i}_modifier`; (5) `procedure_date` = `procedure_{i}_date`; (6) `sequence_number` = `procedure_{i}_priority`; (7) `procedure_type` = `procedure_{i}_type`; (8) `codeset_system` = `lit('HCPCS')` (always the literal 'HCPCS'). The `procedure_{i}_type` value itself was computed during the wide pivot via a nested CASE: `CASE WHEN is_principal_proc = 'Y' THEN 'Principal' ELSE 'Secondary' END` (wrapped in the `MAX(CASE WHEN proc_rank = i THEN ... END)` pivot). Note: unlike `other_diagnoses`, `other_procedures` is NOT wrapped in `array_sort` — it is filtered but left in rank order.

questions.question: The `service_locations` column is an `array<struct>` with a single element. Which of its fields carry real source data versus placeholder NULLs, and what is each real field sourced from?
questions.reference_answer: `service_locations = array(struct(...))` — exactly one struct element. The struct has ~32 fields, but only FOUR carry real source data (after the leading `reference_id` which is a `lit(None).cast('string')` placeholder): (1) `facility_npi` = `col('rendering_facility_npi_prov').cast('string')` (from claim_provider, _prov suffix); (2) `facility_name` = `col('rendering_facility_name_prov')` (claim_provider); (3) `facility_type_code` = `col('facility_type_code_prov')` (claim_provider); (4) `place_of_service_code` = `col('place_of_service_code_hdr')` (claim_header, _hdr suffix). Every remaining field — `facility_taxonomy_code`, the address block (address_line1/2, city, state, postal_code, county_fips, country_code), latitude/longitude, phone/fax/email, contact_name, operational/physical status fields, managing-org fields, endpoint_url, and the identifier_* fields — is set to `lit(None)` cast to its type (string/double), i.e. placeholders populated later by the facility-enrichment pipeline. So 3 real fields come from claim_provider and 1 from claim_header; the rest are NULL placeholders plus the NULL reference_id.

questions.question: The `other_amounts` column is an `array<struct>` of name/value pairs. How many entries does it contain, what is the struct shape, and what are the source columns for the COB-derived and interest entries specifically?
questions.reference_answer: `other_amounts = array(struct(...), ...)` with TWELVE entries. Each entry is a struct of two fields: `name` (a string literal label) and `value` (`col(...).cast('decimal(18,2)')`). The 12 (name -> source column) pairs are: billed_amount -> `billed_amount_hdr`; allowed_amount -> `allowed_amount_hdr`; paid_amount -> `total_paid_amount_cob`; contractual_adjustment -> `total_contractual_adj_cob`; cob_allowed_amount -> `cob_allowed_amount_cob`; cob_billed_amount -> `cob_billed_amount_cob`; patient_liability -> `cob_patient_liability_cob`; copay_amount -> `cob_copay_amount_cob`; deductible_amount -> `cob_deductible_amount_cob`; interest_amount -> `total_interest_amount`; coinsurance_amount -> `coinsurance_amount_hdr`; member_responsibility -> `member_responsibility_hdr`. The COB-derived entries (paid_amount, contractual_adjustment, cob_allowed_amount, cob_billed_amount, patient_liability, copay_amount, deductible_amount) all come from the `_cob`-suffixed columns produced by the aggregated_cob SQL CTE (which COALESCEd them to 0). The interest entry (`interest_amount`) comes from `total_interest_amount`, the SUM produced by `interest_agg_df`. The remaining (billed/allowed/coinsurance/member_responsibility) come from the `_hdr` claim_header columns. All values are cast to decimal(18,2).

questions.question: What is the purpose and shape of `extension_source_values`, how many entries does it have, and is any of its entries sourced from a DERIVED (pipeline-computed) column rather than a raw bronze column?
questions.reference_answer: `extension_source_values` is an `array<struct>` of name/value audit pairs recording which source fed each key business attribute (used downstream by FHIR ExplanationOfBenefit extension jobs to audit provenance). It has FIFTEEN entries; each struct has `name` (string literal) and `value` (`col(...).cast('string')`). The entries map: claim_id->claim_id_hdr, claim_line_id->claim_line_id_hdr, member_id->member_id_hdr, subscriber_id->subscriber_id_hdr, billing_npi->billing_npi_prov, rendering_npi->rendering_npi, claim_type->claim_type_hdr, type_of_bill->type_of_bill_hdr, place_of_service->place_of_service_code_hdr, product_code->product_code_hdr, plan_id->plan_id, payer_id->payer_id, primary_diag_code->primary_diag_code_hdr, admit_status->admit_status_hdr, provider_specialty_code->provider_specialty_code. YES — several entries are sourced from DERIVED columns, not raw bronze: `plan_id` and `payer_id` are pipeline-computed via the product_code when-chains; `provider_specialty_code` is the signal-precedence when-chain result; and `rendering_npi` comes from the provider_specialty SQL rollup. So the audit array deliberately captures both raw header values and pipeline-derived values.

questions.question: How is `claim_outcome` derived from `claim_status_hdr`? Give the complete mapping including the default, and state how its default differs from `processing_status`'s default.
questions.reference_answer: `claim_outcome` is a first-match `when`-chain on `claim_status_hdr`: 'Adjudicated' -> 'complete'; 'Denied' -> 'complete'; 'Pended' -> 'queued'; 'Suspended' -> 'error'; 'Voided' -> 'complete'; 'Adjusted' -> 'partial'; `.otherwise(lit(None))`. So three statuses (Adjudicated, Denied, Voided) map to 'complete', and Pended/Suspended/Adjusted map to queued/error/partial respectively. Crucially the DEFAULT differs from `processing_status`: `claim_outcome.otherwise` is `lit(None)` (unknown statuses produce NULL), whereas `processing_status.otherwise` is `lit('active')` (unknown statuses default to 'active'). Both columns are driven by the same source column `claim_status_hdr`, so a change to the claim_status vocabulary affects both — but an unrecognized status yields processing_status='active' and claim_outcome=NULL.

questions.question: Describe the `'Emergency / Observation'` category predicate. What two parts must hold, what revenue codes / type-of-bill pattern are checked, and how is the admit-status condition expressed?
questions.reference_answer: `cond_er_obs` is a compound AND of two parts: (A) a non-elective admit check, and (B) an ER/Observation revenue-or-TOB check. Part A: `F.coalesce(F.col('admit_status_hdr'), F.lit('')) != F.lit('1')` — i.e. admit_status is NOT '1' (elective), with NULL coalesced to '' so a missing admit_status counts as non-elective (passes A). Part B is an OR of two conditions: (B1) `exists(revenue_code_list, x -> x is not null AND trim(x) != '' AND lpad(regexp_replace(trim(x), '[^0-9]', ''), 4, '0') IN ('0762','0450'))` — any revenue code normalizing to 0762 (observation) or 0450 (emergency room); OR (B2) `upper(trim(type_of_bill_hdr)) LIKE '13%'` — Type of Bill starting with 13 (hospital outpatient). A claim is Emergency/Observation iff A AND (B1 OR B2). The revenue-code normalization (trim, strip non-digits via regexp_replace, lpad to 4 with '0') is the same pattern used by the Rehab and Hospice predicates, only with a different code set.

questions.question: What is the `'Durable Medical Equipment'` category predicate? Which columns and values does it test?
questions.reference_answer: `cond_dme` is a two-branch OR: `(F.col('place_of_service_code_hdr') == F.lit('12')) | (F.upper(F.trim(F.col('claim_type_hdr'))) == F.lit('DME'))`. A claim qualifies as Durable Medical Equipment iff EITHER the place-of-service code equals '12' (Home) OR the claim_type (uppercased and trimmed) equals 'DME'. It is the only category predicate that keys off place_of_service_code_hdr and claim_type_hdr, and unlike the TOB-based predicates it does not use any revenue-code or LIKE-pattern test. Note the place-of-service comparison is an exact string match on '12' (not trimmed/uppered), while the claim_type side is upper+trim normalized.

questions.question: Compare the `'Home Health'` and `'Skilled Nursing Facility'` category predicates. What Type-of-Bill patterns does each test, and is there a difference in how the type_of_bill string is normalized before the LIKE?
questions.reference_answer: Both are Type-of-Bill (TOB) pattern tests but they normalize differently. Home Health (`cond_home_health`): `F.upper(F.trim(F.col('type_of_bill_hdr'))).like('32%') | F.upper(F.trim(F.col('type_of_bill_hdr'))).like('33%')` — TOB starting with 32 OR 33, with the string UPPERCASED and trimmed first. Skilled Nursing Facility (`cond_snf`): `F.trim(F.col('type_of_bill_hdr')).like('21%')` — TOB starting with 21, but only TRIMMED (NO `upper()`). So the difference: Home Health applies `upper(trim(...))`, whereas SNF applies only `trim(...)` before the LIKE. SNF tests a single pattern '21%'; Home Health tests two patterns '32%' and '33%'. (Since TOB codes are numeric the missing upper() on SNF is harmless in practice, but the normalization is genuinely different in the code.)

questions.question: The pipeline applies `suffix_rename` to some source DataFrames but not others. Which DataFrames get a suffix, which join inputs deliberately do NOT, and how do the un-suffixed ones still join correctly?
questions.reference_answer: `suffix_rename(df, suffix)` uses `df.toDF(*[c+suffix for c in df.columns])` to append a suffix to every column. It is applied to FIVE DataFrames: `claim_hdr_df` ('_hdr'), `claim_prov_df` ('_prov'), `member_df` ('_mbr'), `aggregated_cob_df` ('_cob'), and `claim_interest_df` ('_int'). It is NOT applied to: `claim_diag_df`, `claim_proc_df`, `claim_occ_df`, `claim_payable_df`, or `provider_df`. How the un-suffixed ones still work: (a) claim_diag_df and claim_proc_df keep their original column names and are joined to the header on `claim_hdr_df['claim_id_hdr'] == claim_diag_df['claim_id']` (and similarly claim_proc) — they are immediately consumed by the wide PIVOTs, whose outputs are then renamed to `claim_id_diag` / `claim_id_proc` for the cascade; (b) claim_occ_df is aggregated separately and its key renamed `claim_id` -> `claim_id_occ`; (c) claim_payable_df is referenced only inside the aggregated_cob `spark.sql` CTE (by table name, not as a Python DataFrame join), so it never needs Python-side suffixing; (d) provider_df is used only inside the provider_specialty `spark.sql` block (joined by SQL alias `pr`). So suffixing is applied exactly to the DataFrames that participate in the Python cascade join where column-name collisions would otherwise occur.

questions.question: How are `plan_id` and `payer_id` derived, what column drives them, and how do their value mappings relate to each other and to `coverage_plans.policy_id`?
questions.reference_answer: Both `plan_id` and `payer_id` are first-match `when`-chains keyed on the SAME source column `product_code_hdr`, with four branches plus an otherwise. `plan_id`: MERIDIAN_PPO -> 'MRD-PPO-001', MERIDIAN_HMO -> 'MRD-HMO-001', MERIDIAN_EPO -> 'MRD-EPO-001', MERIDIAN_DSNP -> 'MRD-DSNP-001', otherwise 'UNKNOWN'. `payer_id`: MERIDIAN_PPO -> '1234567890', MERIDIAN_HMO -> '1234567891', MERIDIAN_EPO -> '1234567892', MERIDIAN_DSNP -> '1234567893', otherwise 'UNKNOWN'. So they share identical branch CONDITIONS (the four product codes) but emit different value sets (plan code strings vs 10-digit payer IDs). Relationship to coverage_plans: `coverage_plans[0].policy_id` is `concat_ws('_', coalesce(member_uid,'UNKNOWN'), coalesce(<the plan_id when-chain repeated INLINE>, 'UNKNOWN'))` — i.e. it re-derives the plan_id mapping inline rather than referencing the plan_id column, so a change to the product_code -> plan code mapping must be made in two places to stay consistent. (coverage_plans also carries payer_id via `coalesce(col('payer_id'), 'UNKNOWN')`, this time referencing the computed payer_id column.)

questions.question: The final projection adds three ETL/audit columns: `etl_loaded_at`, `etl_source_job`, and `source_system`. How is each produced, and which one is non-deterministic across runs?
questions.reference_answer: All three are added inside the final `silver_df = final_df.select(...)` projection as non-source-derived columns: `etl_loaded_at = F.current_timestamp().alias('etl_loaded_at')`; `etl_source_job = F.lit('silver_clinical_claims').alias('etl_source_job')`; `source_system = F.lit('meridian').alias('source_system')`. Two are constants (`etl_source_job` = literal 'silver_clinical_claims', `source_system` = literal 'meridian'), so they have no upstream lineage. The NON-DETERMINISTIC one is `etl_loaded_at`: `current_timestamp()` is evaluated at run time, so the same input data yields a different value on each run. A lineage tool should represent etl_loaded_at as derived from a runtime function (no source column) and the other two as literal constants.

questions.question: Two output columns are both derived from `claim_status_hdr`. Name them, and explain why a change to the claim_status code vocabulary in `bronze.claim_header` would affect both.
questions.reference_answer: The two columns are `processing_status` and `claim_outcome`. Both are independent first-match `when`-chains whose conditions all test the SAME source column `claim_status_hdr` (values 'Adjudicated','Denied','Pended','Suspended','Voided','Adjusted'). `processing_status` maps them to a FHIR ClaimResponse.status value set (Adjudicated/Denied/Adjusted -> 'active', Pended/Suspended -> 'draft', Voided -> 'cancelled', otherwise -> 'active'); `claim_outcome` maps them to ClaimResponse.outcome (Adjudicated/Denied/Voided -> 'complete', Pended -> 'queued', Suspended -> 'error', Adjusted -> 'partial', otherwise -> NULL). Because both read only `claim_status_hdr`, any change to the claim_status vocabulary (a renamed code, a new status value, or a removed one) propagates to BOTH outputs simultaneously: a new unmapped status would fall through to processing_status='active' and claim_outcome=NULL. They are the file's example of one source column fanning out to two derived columns.

questions.question: Describe the window used to rank procedures for the wide pivot in the procedure stage. Give its full PARTITION BY / ORDER BY spec, the ranking function, and how `procedure_<i>_type` is determined within the pivot.
questions.reference_answer: The procedure window is `proc_rank_window = Window.partitionBy('claim_id_hdr').orderBy(F.col('proc_priority').asc_nulls_last(), F.col('hcpcs_code').asc_nulls_last())`, applied as `row_number().over(proc_rank_window)` to produce `proc_rank` on `ranked_proc_df` (claim_hdr LEFT JOIN claim_proc on claim_id). Partition: `claim_id_hdr` (one ranking per claim). Sort: `proc_priority` ASCENDING nulls-last, tie-broken by `hcpcs_code` ASCENDING nulls-last — so the lowest-priority-number (most significant) procedure, then lowest HCPCS code, becomes rank 1. MAX_PROC=4, so the pivot keeps ranks 1..4 via `MAX(CASE WHEN proc_rank = i THEN ... END)`. `procedure_{i}_type` is determined inside the pivot by a nested CASE: `MAX(CASE WHEN proc_rank = i THEN CASE WHEN is_principal_proc = 'Y' THEN 'Principal' ELSE 'Secondary' END END)` — i.e. the rank-i procedure is labeled 'Principal' if its is_principal_proc flag is 'Y', else 'Secondary'. This window mirrors the diagnosis window's structure (same partition key, ASC-nulls-last two-key sort, row_number) but orders by proc_priority/hcpcs_code instead of diag_priority/icd10_code, and keeps 4 ranks instead of 5.

questions.question: How is the boolean column `is_pcp_claim` derived, and what is its signal precedence? How does it relate to the PCP logic in `provider_specialty_code`?
questions.reference_answer: `is_pcp_claim` is a `coalesce` of three boolean signals in precedence order: `coalesce(F.col('is_pcp_eligible_reg').cast('boolean'), (F.col('any_pcp_flag') == F.lit(1)), F.lit(False))`. Precedence: (1) the primary rendering provider's registry PCP flag `is_pcp_eligible_reg` (cast to boolean) if non-null; (2) else whether ANY rendering provider on the claim is PCP-eligible, expressed as `any_pcp_flag == 1` (any_pcp_flag is the MAX(CASE WHEN is_pcp_eligible=true THEN 1 ELSE 0) aggregate from the any_pcp_signal CTE); (3) else `False`. Relationship to `provider_specialty_code`: the same two PCP signals drive the top of that column's when-chain — if `coalesce(is_pcp_eligible_reg cast boolean, False) == True` OR `coalesce(any_pcp_flag,0) == 1`, provider_specialty_code is set to the literal 'PCP' (overriding the registry/claim specialty codes). So is_pcp_claim is the boolean form of the same PCP-touched logic that forces provider_specialty_code='PCP'; both prefer the top-ranked provider's registry flag and fall back to the claim-wide any_pcp_flag.

questions.question: Both `other_diagnoses` and `other_procedures` are built as filtered arrays of conditional structs. What is the key processing difference between how the two final arrays are produced?
questions.reference_answer: Both are built the same way up to a point: an intermediate `*_raw` column = `array(*[when(col('<code>_i').isNotNull(), struct(...)) ...])` over the ranked wide columns, then a `filter(..., x -> x is not null)` to drop ranks with no code, then the `_raw` column is dropped. The KEY DIFFERENCE is sorting: `other_diagnoses = array_sort(expr("filter(other_diagnoses_raw, x -> x is not null)"))` — it is wrapped in `array_sort`, so the surviving diagnosis structs are sorted (by natural struct ordering). `other_procedures = expr("filter(other_procedures_raw, x -> x is not null)")` — it is NOT wrapped in array_sort, so the surviving procedure structs remain in their original rank order. So diagnoses are filter+SORT; procedures are filter only. (Secondary differences: the diag inner struct has 8 fields with codeset_system='ICD-10-CM' and includes diagnosis_type / present_on_admission_code / diagnosis_group; the proc inner struct has 8 fields with codeset_system='HCPCS' and includes modifier_code / procedure_date / procedure_type — but the question's core answer is the array_sort vs no-sort distinction.)

questions.question: How is the final table partitioned on write, and is there any discrepancy between the partitioning comment and the actual code? What guarantees the partition column is never NULL?
questions.reference_answer: The write is `dq_passed_df.write.format('delta').mode('overwrite').option('overwriteSchema','true').partitionBy('service_from_date').saveAsTable(f'{SILVER}.clinical_claims')` — Delta format, full-refresh overwrite with overwriteSchema, partitioned by `service_from_date`, written to `meridian.silver.clinical_claims`. DISCREPANCY: the comment says the table is 'partitioned by service_from_date (date-truncated to month)', but the actual code calls `.partitionBy('service_from_date')` with NO month truncation — it partitions on the raw service_from_date value, not a month bucket. So the comment overstates/ misdescribes the code. What guarantees no NULL partition: the upstream DQ stage `dq_passed_df` filters `F.col('service_from_date').isNotNull()` (one of its three mandatory not-null filters, alongside claim_id and member_id), so every row reaching the write has a non-null service_from_date — there can be no NULL/default partition.

questions.question: The occurrence codes and interest adjustments are each aggregated to claim grain in their own steps and then joined back. For each, give the group key, the aggregate(s) produced, the renamed join key, and the join condition used in the cascade.
questions.reference_answer:
OCCURRENCE (`occ_agg_df`): built from `claim_occ_df`; first a per-row `occ_struct` = `when(occ_code.isNotNull(), struct(reference_id=lit(None), occurrence_code=occ_code, occurrence_date=occ_date, span_from_date=occ_span_from_date, span_to_date=occ_span_to_date))`; then `.groupBy('claim_id').agg(F.array_distinct(F.collect_list('occ_struct')).alias('occurrence_codes'))`; the key is renamed `claim_id` -> `claim_id_occ`. In the cascade it joins LEFT on `claim_hdr_df['claim_id_hdr'] == occ_agg_df['claim_id_occ']`. So its aggregate is array_distinct(collect_list(struct)) producing the `occurrence_codes` array.
INTEREST (`interest_agg_df`): built from `claim_interest_df` (already _int-suffixed); `.groupBy('claim_id_int').agg(F.sum('interest_amount_int').alias('total_interest_amount'), F.count('interest_amount_int').alias('interest_line_count'))`; the key is renamed `claim_id_int` -> `claim_id_int_agg`. In the cascade it joins LEFT on `claim_hdr_df['claim_id_hdr'] == interest_agg_df['claim_id_int_agg']`. So it produces two aggregates: total_interest_amount (SUM) and interest_line_count (COUNT). Both join-backs are LEFT joins keyed on the claim_header's claim_id_hdr.

questions.question: How are the `BRONZE` and `SILVER` schema prefixes constructed, and does the `MERIDIAN_DATABASE` environment-variable override actually change which catalog/schema the pipeline reads from and writes to? Justify from the code.
questions.reference_answer: `DATABASE = 'meridian'`, `BRONZE = f'{DATABASE}.bronze'` = 'meridian.bronze', `SILVER = f'{DATABASE}.silver'` = 'meridian.silver'. There is also `_env_db = os.environ.get('MERIDIAN_DATABASE', DATABASE)` with an inline comment calling it a 'runtime override hook'. However, the `MERIDIAN_DATABASE` override is INEFFECTIVE: `_env_db` is assigned but NEVER referenced anywhere else in the file. Both BRONZE and SILVER (and therefore every `spark.table(f'{BRONZE}....')` read, the `{BRONZE}` interpolations inside the two `spark.sql` CTE blocks, and the final `saveAsTable(f'{SILVER}.clinical_claims')`) are built from `DATABASE` directly, not from `_env_db`. So setting the MERIDIAN_DATABASE env var has no effect — all reads and the write stay pinned to the literal 'meridian' catalog/schema. A static lineage tool can resolve every table FQN to meridian.bronze.* / meridian.silver.* with certainty regardless of the environment, because the override variable is dead code.

questions.question: Several category predicates reference `revenue_code_list`. Is `revenue_code_list` produced, derived, or read anywhere in this file? What does that imply for tracing its lineage?
questions.reference_answer: `revenue_code_list` is referenced inside `F.expr(...)` in three category predicates — `cond_rehab`, `cond_hospice`, and `cond_er_obs` (each does `exists(revenue_code_list, x -> ...)`). But it is NOT produced anywhere in this file: there is no `withColumn('revenue_code_list', ...)`, it is not in the final canonical projection, and — unlike every other column referenced in those predicates (e.g. `type_of_bill_hdr`, `admit_status_hdr`, `primary_diag_code_hdr`, which all carry the `_hdr` suffix from suffix_rename) — it is referenced WITHOUT any suffix. Since the claim_header columns were all suffixed to `_hdr`, a bare `revenue_code_list` does not correspond to any column this file creates or renames. Implication: `revenue_code_list` has no in-file producer; its origin is unresolved/assumed-preexisting (it would have to arrive on final_df from a source not handled in this file). For lineage this is a GAP — a static tool cannot trace revenue_code_list back to a bronze column from this file, and should flag it as an unresolved column reference used by three classification predicates. (At runtime this reference would not resolve against the suffixed header columns, making it a latent issue as well.)

questions.question: `MAX_DIAG = 5` controls the diagnosis pivot. If it were changed to 3, what specifically would change in the generated columns and the `other_diagnoses` array — and why would the final projection break?
questions.reference_answer: `MAX_DIAG` drives two loops: (a) `diag_pivot_exprs` is built with `for i in range(1, MAX_DIAG + 1)`, generating five sets of wide pivot columns `diagnosis_1_*` .. `diagnosis_5_*` (code/description/type/poa/priority); (b) `diag_structs` is built with the same range, producing five conditional structs that feed `other_diagnoses_raw = array(*diag_structs)` and then `other_diagnoses`. If MAX_DIAG were changed to 3: only `diagnosis_1_*` .. `diagnosis_3_*` wide columns would be generated, and `other_diagnoses` would consider only the top 3 ranks (its array would hold at most 3 structs). The FINAL PROJECTION WOULD BREAK: `silver_df = final_df.select(...)` explicitly lists `col('diagnosis_4_code')` and `col('diagnosis_5_code')` (the canonical contract hardcodes diagnoses 1-5). With MAX_DIAG=3 those two columns are never created, so the `.select` would raise an AnalysisException for the missing `diagnosis_4_code` / `diagnosis_5_code`. So MAX_DIAG is implicitly coupled to the hardcoded 1-5 projection: changing it requires editing the final select too. (The Maternity predicate `cond_maternity` also references diagnosis_1_code..diagnosis_5_code explicitly, so it would likewise reference now-missing columns.) Lineage-wise, lowering MAX_DIAG removes the rank-4 and rank-5 derive edges and the other_diagnoses contributions from those ranks.
